newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina says facing minor U.S. patent sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Argentina says facing minor U.S. patent sanctions.

text.p: The United States is about to announce minor reprisals against Argentina for patents legislation it says does not protect drugs firms sufficiently from bootleggers, a Foreign Ministry spokeswoman said Wednesday.

The United States wrote a letter to the Argentine government advising that it would remove 50 percent of benefits it currently grants to Argentina under its general preference scheme for imports, the spokeswoman told Reuters.
The measure will probably be enacted in April, after a 30-day period for questions.
Local newspapers reported that the U.S. move would cost Argentina between $10 million and $20 million a year, and government officials minimized the effects on exports.
Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella said Monday that the United States was planning some action.
He said that the sanctions would group Argentina with some nations it does not usually like to associate with, but that they were ineffectual.
"It puts us in a pestilent category (of nations), but it's neither here nor there to us," Di Tella told reporters.
The U.S. move would be would be the first real action by the United States to chastise Argentina for its patent laws, after years of public haranguing.

Patents have long been a point of discord in the otherwise cozy relations between Argentina and the United States. Washington says foreign pharmaceutical firms lose $500 million a year in Argentina to bootleggers.

The goverment of President Carlos Menem undertook a marathon struggle with Congress -- strongly lobbied by Argentina's own pharmaceutical industry -- to update intellectual property laws and appease the United States. But, while the bill was eventually passed and beefed up with extra confidentiality rules, the United States still feels it is insufficient.
